body.text: Sikyong Penpa Tsering is the democratically elected leader of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), the Tibetan government in exile based in India. In mid-November, the sikyong visited Washington, DC, where he sat down for an interview with The Diplomat’s Shannon Tiezzi. They discussed the CTA’s vision for Tibet, the prospect of dialogue with China and the importance of international support.
A transcript of the interview, edited for length and clarity, is below. You can view the full interview on YouTube.
Shannon Tiezzi: I will jump right in by asking for your thoughts on the current state of U.S.-Tibet relations, especially given your visit to Washington, DC.

Sikyong Penpa Tsering: I think because of the leadership of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, who always stressed that supporting Tibet is not necessarily anti-China, but it’s supporting truth and justice, we have always had very good bipartisan support in the Congress, bicameral support in the Congress, and also from the state. So this continues even today. So I would say it’s status quo from where we were and where we are going.
Do you feel that the recent high profile engagements between President Trump and China’s Xi Jinping have impacted the U.S.-Tibet relationship?

We have not seen any visible impact. As I mentioned, it’s status quo. There are a lot of things on the table between the United States and China at the moment. And some of the important issues that concerns the United States, like fentanyl has also gone out of the agenda. New areas like AI and denuclearization are also coming into focus.
We have not seen any major visible changes on Tibet cause because of President Xi and Trump’s meeting. So we continue to receive good support both from the Congress and the state.

We’re seeing renewed dialogue between the U.S. and China right now. Do you see a real possibility of dialogue between the CTA and China, or between Tibetan leadership in perhaps other formats and the government in Beijing?

I have always said that we do have some kind of a back channel which are inconsequential, leading to reestablishment of contact or negotiation. If you look at what China is doing in Tibet and the whole of China, there is no political space right now. So as long as there is no sensible leadership at the helm of Chinese affairs, we don’t expect any breakthrough.

Of course, China keeps talking about dialogue and negotiation when it comes to international conflicts. They have no dialogue with the Tibetans; they have no dialogue with the Taiwanese. They always try to repress us. They try to choke our reach to the international community.
I’m just coming from Holland before this visit and the Foreign Affairs Committee with whom I had a session, they also received what we call as a love letter from the Chinese embassy.

So there is always pressure from the Chinese government, wherever they have the leverage, with whomever they have diplomatic relations or trade relations, then they force these countries to stop access for the Tibetans or Uyghurs or other stakeholders which have a problem with China.

Wherever they feel they can put pressure on governments, they put pressure. So governments also realize that once you deal with China, it doesn’t come for free. Your sovereignty also comes into question as to whether you can take your own position.

The Chinese government always keeps saying that Tibet is a domestic issue, but I always tell them Tibet is not a domestic issue. Tibet historically was an independent state. Till the occupation of Tibet by China in 1950, you will not find anywhere in any history, whether it’s Indian history or Nepalese history or Bhutanese history or any neighboring countries of Tibet, about India-China border. It never was there. It was always India-Tibetan border, Nepal-Tibet border, Bhutan-Tibet border, not the way it is now.

Despite our historical rights or rights under international law, we are asking for the “Middle Way,” genuine autonomy for the Tibetans, because His Holiness always appreciates the larger interests of humanity, even though we were an independent nation.

China keeps saying that Tibet has been part of China since antiquity, time immemorial, which is not the truth. If you can consider the Mongol Yuan as Chinese or the Manchu Qing as Chinese, Tibet has never been ruled by China historically. So it’s not a domestic issue. It is still an international issue that international community can definitely talk about it and speak about it.

What China is doing is where they have the leverage, they put pressure on governments and the governments also realize it. Even in Latin America, when I was in Mexico, I was supposed to meet with the president of Guadalajara and Chinese government put pressure saying that if you meet with Penpa then the metro project will be gone. So that’s how they put pressure.

You mentioned the Middle Way and autonomy. China often refers to the CTA and even His Holiness the Dalai Lama, as splittists, people who are seeking Tibetan independence. Could you tell us in your own words what the CTA’s long-term vision is for Tibet?

We are still committed to nonviolence as a means to resolve conflicts. China is not responding to the pragmatic approach of His Holiness the Dalai Lama seeking genuine autonomy. China keeps calling His Holiness a separatist. So His Holiness keeps chanting like a mantra: autonomy, autonomy, autonomy, Middle Way, Middle Way, and China keeps calling him a splittist, separatist.
So I question the Chinese government as to who really wants Tibet to be separated from China. Is it the Chinese government or His Holiness the Dalai Lama who’s seeking autonomy, not independence?

I came into this position [of sikyong] in 2021; this is my second term. Just at the beginning of my second term [in May 2026], we changed our strategy a little bit to focus on the ends – when His Holiness speaks about the middle, then there are ends. So one end is the historical status of Tibet as an independent state. And the other end is the current situation of occupied Tibet under the repressive communist government.

What concerns the Chinese government is sovereignty. The United States adopted the Resolve Tibet Act in 2024. If more like-minded countries adopt this position, then there would be leverage and value for the Middle Way that might force China to come on the negotiating table. And that is the strategy we are following now, focusing on the ends and then gain leverage for the Middle Way, hoping that Chinese government will respond to our pragmatic approach.

As I’m sure most of our viewers are aware, China has been moving in the opposite direction. Rather than increased autonomy, there’s been growing repression, not just in Tibet, but in many other ethnic regions, especially since the ethnic unity law entered into force. How is this factoring into your work and how is it impacting the Tibetan people not just within the Tibetan region, but the diaspora around the world?

That’s why I keep saying we are dying a slow death. It’s like we normally talk about being strangled by a python. In our case, we are being strangled by the dragon, slowly but surely. So what China is doing in Tibet amounts to a certain level of genocide, at least cultural genocide, with this so-called ethnic unity and progress law, which they adopted on March 12 this year and supposed to be implementing from July 1. They have been implementing all these programs for the last more than at least 10 years in the form of colonial style boarding schools, restrictions on monastic religious institutions, our way of life, our culture, every aspect of Tibetan life.

And you know, Wang Huning is the ideologue behind this since 2011. He has been saying that if there are no nationalities, there won’t be nationality issues. So how do you make sure that there are no nationalities? You can’t kill all the Tibetans. You can’t kill all the East Turkestanis or Uyghurs. You cannot kill all the Mongols. So the way forward for them is assimilation.

Even four-year-old kids are being sent to boarding schools away from their family, away from their culture, away from their language, away from their way of life. And I think there’s also a certain level of indoctrination going on, saying that your culture is backward, your language is backward. Even four-year-old kids who are sent to colonial Montessori schools; when they come home for holidays, they don’t speak in Tibetan anymore. So this will be very consequential for the Tibetans.

The whole world’s working towards preserving heritage, civilizations, and all that, but China is bent on destroying the civilizational and national identity of the Tibetans and Uyghurs and Mongols. So I really wonder what they gain from this. They want to create a common Chinese community for the Chinese nation. Just speak one language.

Even Buddhism, they say, with Chinese characteristic, what do they mean? They have gained control of all the monastic institutions. The number of monks and nuns have come down. The control and surveillance in the monasteries has gone up. The Chinese government, who does not believe in any religion, wants to be responsible for setting up curriculum and monastic study alongside expressing allegiance to the Communist Party and the leadership.

Sometimes I say that maybe George Orwell must be rolling in his grave if he finds that China has mastered the fine art of control and surveillance much beyond his imagination. And now they want to be responsible for reincarnation of lamas as early as 2007 when they laid this law called Order No. 5.

So it’s not rule of law, it’s rule by law. They have this anti-separatist law against the Taiwanese because of which they are not able to amend their constitution, which would be construed as declaring independence and inviting the wrath of the Chinese government. For the Hong Kongers and Macau, they have the national security law. Now you know what is happening under those laws where people are being incriminated and imprisoned, including Jimmy Lai.

And for the Tibetans and Uyghurs and Mongols now they have this so-called ethnic unity and progress law. So it’s just given the force of law to use all apparatus of the government to implement this law which contradicts with the 1984 national regional autonomy law under the provision of the 1982 constitution, which if you read you will find that must be one of the best constitutions of the world. But that’s not what they use. They use the Communist Party’s charter.
I always say that what China is doing in Tibet, in East Turkestan, in Mongolia, the whole of China is a template of what they want to do to the whole world.

You mentioned the Chinese Communist Party’s push to, as they call it, “sinicize” religions, including Buddhism, and the implications for China’s control over the reincarnation process. I think this has really gained the world’s attention. As the Dalai Lama celebrates a birthday each year, there’s a renewed focus on what happens when it’s time for the reincarnation of the Dalai Lama. Most analysts think that China’s going to select its own CCP-approved Dalai Lama. So what is the CTA’s plan for countering that and making sure that this remains a religious process rather than a political one?

China is already accusing us of politicizing the reincarnation issue, which they themselves are doing for their political gain. We all know that China is a communist government. They don’t believe in any religion, they are repressing Buddhism in Tibet, but they are focusing a lot on reincarnation. Why so? Because they believe that if they can control the next Dalai Lama, then they can control the whole of Tibet, which is the largest open prison in the world today. And then Tibet would no more be an international issue after the demise of the 14th Dalai Lama.

So his Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama keeps saying that I will live long, very long. And there are also propitious presigns that he will live long. So I tell that to the Chinese: this message is for you because you are waiting for this Dalai Lama to die. Now let us see whether His Holiness the Dalai Lama outlives the Communist Party or the Communist Party outlives His Holiness the Dalai Lama.
His Holiness has very simple responses to China’s positions.

One, that they will look for His Holiness reincarnation within China. Which means they have no understanding of how the reincarnation process works and what it’s meant for. They are ordering the Dalai Lama, who is the one to decide where he will be born, to not be born outside China or Tibet. So His Holiness’ response is very simple: I will be born in a free world. It’s he who’s going to decide where he will be, not the communist government.

And the second position is the Chinese government says that we have to use the golden urn, which they used as a political tool when they choose the 11th Panchen. You know the story, the real Panchen, the six-year-old boy way back in 1995, was chosen by His Holiness Dalai Lama and he disappeared along with his family. We still don’t know where he is.
They [the Chinese government] chose their own Panchen Lama. Now they are sending him more and more into Tibet because they want to use him as a tool to choose the next Dalai Lama.

Tibetans inside Tibet, if you ask about this Chinese Panchen, they would say he’s just another leader. They won’t recognize him as the true reincarnation of the 10th Panchen Lama. Similarly, whatever Chinese government does in terms of choosing the 14 Dalai Lama, no Tibetans in their right mind who are truly Buddhist will accept China’s selection at all.

His Holiness always has a very humorous response to difficult questions by saying, if the Chinese government are really serious, they should study Tibetan Buddhism, believe in the concept of life and death. And if they’re still more serious, they should look for Mao Zedong’s reincarnation first. Then Deng Xiaoping’s reincarnation second, and then maybe Jiang Zemin, then maybe the Dalai Lamas.

Because sometimes you feel like the Chinese leaders also want to be worshipped, even though they’re atheists. You find Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, and Hu Jintao, alongside Tibetan Buddhist statues. So this is again a paradox of what China is doing.

It’s ridiculous, even blasphemers of Chinese government that does not believe in any religion to interfere in the sacred tradition of selective reincarnation, which is very unique to Tibetan Buddhism. We have been practicing this for more than last 900 years.

They might try. We are prepared. His Holiness has already issued a statement on July 2nd, 2025, just before his 90th birthday. So we will follow this tradition. And if China wants a lifelong headache, so be it.

So clearly there are a lot of challenges to face for the Tibetan people. What do you see as the best case scenario for Tibets, based on all the constraints that are posed by the Chinese Communist Party and the difficulties of the Tibetan people around the world?
We only hope that the present leadership becomes more sensible.

All we need is a more sensible leadership in China. Despite Tibet’s historical rights, despite Tibet’s rights under international law, His Holiness is not asking for independence; he is asking for autonomy. And if Chinese leadership really respects people, then they should accept the pragmatic approach of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, give the Tibetans the right to use their language, practice its religion, preserve its culture, and promote its way of life, including protection of Tibet’s environment.

So we only hope that a sensible leadership comes at the helm of Chinese affairs and then gives genuine autonomy or real autonomy – not the name Tibet Autonomous Region, Tibet Autonomous Prefecture, Tibet Autonomous County where there’s no real autonomy. That is why His Holiness is asking for genuine autonomy.

And we also know for a fact that if there could be any resolution to the Tibet conflict, it can come only from China. It’s not going to come from NATO; it’s not going to fight for Tibet. India is not going to fight for Tibet; Japan is not going to fight for Tibet. We don’t believe in violence. We believe in non-violence. We believe in a negotiated solution. We believe in a mutually beneficial solution that would be lasting.

Nonviolence is the only means if you want a more secure future for the future generations of humanity – not just for Tibetans, but to all the people who are facing repressive regimes around the world.

If we are able to go back to Tibet in any form, we have to live with China as our neighbors. We have lived with Chinese as our neighbors for centuries; with Indians, Nepalese, Bhutanese. So if we have to live as neighbors, then why not live in peace with each other?
